section: How do we make data analysis agents trustworthy?
text:
How do we make data analysis agents trustworthy?

so if models still are going to make mistakes and we have this context problem, how can we make data agents give us the right answers? how can we make them trustworthy?

Two problems

  
    The model has to write the right code.
  
  
    The user has to know how trustworthy the code is.
  


and we actually have two problems
we need the model to run the right code, but if we know that it sometimes won’t, we need a way to communicate levels of trust we have in that code to the user ESPECIALLY if that user isn’t a data scientist themselves

commons does 3 things

Extract trusted calculations from existing artifacts into a data structure
A harness to give the right context at the right time
A feedback loop to push more queries up the trust ladder over time

Let’s see it in action
The first thing the agent does is search for a trusted calculation. Here it finds and runs a trusted site traffic calculation.
The answer is marked as verified to signify that it used vetted code.

However, it’s unlikely that trusted code will cover all questions a user might have. For these situations, the agent can write custom R, Python, or SQL.
First, the agent looks through additional context in the form of data dictionaries, markdown files, and, if you have them, existing context layers from Databricks and Snowflake.
Then, it writes whatever code it needs to find an answer.
Finally, when it presents an answer, it can provide a citation to that context. The citation is deterministically checked against trusted context that has appeared in the conversation – if it matches, a citation tag is shown.

There’s one more possible path: the model cannot find trusted context to justify its approach. In this case, we mark the answer with a yellow tag, which lets the user know the answer should be considered less trusted.
The tool has to feel convenient enough that the user actually wants to reach for it – it needs to feel like a normal chat. When correctness is closer to a normal coding agent, we signal that the user ought to be more skeptical of the answer.

Two problems

  
    The model has to write the right code.
    Trusted calculations and organizational context
  
  
    The user has to know how trustworthy the code is.
    Trust tags and verified citations
  


Trusted calculations and context help with the first problem. tags and checked citations make the answer’s grounding visible for the second.

commons deterministically tags the trust level. This isn’t decided by the model. Question: why not have the model assign the trust levels?
models are great performers

The answers look the same




 ❌


 ✅


 ❌




The problem with this performance just that the model is sometimes wrong, it’s that the wrong answers are confident and can be indistinguishable from the right ones
we have a clearly parabolic plot and three descriptions from the same model shared tone, shared style, shared length – but different description each time if you didn’t know what the plot looked like, you wouldn’t be able to disentangle the correct ones from the incorrect ones
we also did one experiment where we asked the model to report its confidence level…always said ~95%

Search trusted calculations
  
    Find one↓
    Don’t find one↓
  
  
    
      Run trusted calculation
      ↓
      
        
      
    
    
      Search context
      ↓
      Write SQL/R/Python
      
        Cite↓
        Don’t cite↓
      
      
        
          
        
        
          
        
      
    
  


Commons records which tools produced the answer. Trust is based on that execution path, not on the model’s confidence in its own answer. trust is deterministic
The citation itself is checked against trusted context. A custom answer is not promoted merely because the model says it used a trusted source.

DevRel Agent


https://github.com/posit-dev/devrel-agent


Live demo: https://posit-devrel-agent.share.connect.posit.cloud/

Build
You construct the agent by hooking it up to trusted code.


Deploy
Your colleagues use the agent deployed on Connect.


Improve
You review the agent’s behavior, adding trusted code to cover common use cases.



After seeing the agents in action, what does this look like for the person building and maintaining them?
Build: connect vetted calculations, data, and organizational context. Deploy: make the agent available to collaborators, for example on Connect. Improve: review its behavior and add calculations or context for recurring questions.

Build: the commons skill

Use a coding agent plus the built-in commons skill to parse through your data and code and build a commons agent.


https://posit-dev.github.io/commons/r/articles/commons.html#working-with-the-agent-skill


The commons package ships as a skill for coding agents (Posit Assistant, Claude Code, Codex).

Information Layers

Photo: Olga Petnyunene, Unsplash

Build: information layers


These layers complement the data source. The semantic layer supplies trusted ways to compute answers. The context layer helps the agent write custom SQL or R and interpret the results when a trusted calculation doesn’t cover the question.
Data dictionaries can contribute to both: calculation definitions to the semantic layer, and descriptive information to the context layer.

Build: information layers


Trusted calculations specify how an answer is computed. Define vetted R or Python functions as measures in scripts.
The semantic layer collects the vetted calculations the agent prefers to use. Functions documented with @measure become measures; the roxygen description and @param tags become the tool’s description and arguments.
The enrollment example uses illustrative definitions. The point is to reuse the team’s calculation rather than have the model reinvent its logic for each question. Measures can contain ordinary R code; they do not have to contain SQL or a dbGetQuery call. The same trusted calculations can also come from data dictionary definitions, Snowflake semantic views, or Databricks metric views.

Build: information layers


The context layer explains what the data means and how to interpret it.
Markdown files and descriptive entries in data dictionaries supply context: what columns mean, terminology, conventions, and limitations.
Data dictionaries can serve both layers: descriptive fields supply context, while calculation definitions supply the semantic layer.

Build
Putting the pieces together

library(commons)

commons <- commons(
  data_sources = data_source(trials = trials),
  semantic_layer = semantic_layer("R/measures.R"),
  context_layer = context_layer(files = "context/protocol-conventions.md")
)

agent <- agent(
  ellmer::chat_anthropic(),
  commons = commons
)

commons_app(agent)


This assembles a chat client, data source, semantic layer, and context layer. The commons() object gathers trusted code and context, and agent() wraps it with trusted-calculation tools, context search, provenance marking, and a sandboxed R session.
The data source here is a data frame (a clinical trials table), which commons loads into an in-process DuckDB database. The semantic and context layers are optional and grow over time – start with a small working scope and expand.
The R/measures.R and context/protocol-conventions.md paths illustrate existing files that supply vetted R measures and organizational context. This is not a self-contained runnable example without those files and its data.

Build
Databricks and Snowflake

# Snowflake semantic view
warehouse <- data_source(
  snowflake_con, tables = "ANALYTICS.TRIAL_ENROLLMENT"
)

# Or: Databricks metric view
warehouse <- data_source(
  databricks_con, tables = "clinical.trial_enrollment_metrics"
)

commons <- commons(
  data_sources = list(warehouse = warehouse),
  context_layer = context_layer(files = "context/protocol-conventions.md")
)

agent <- agent(
  ellmer::chat_anthropic(),
  commons = commons
)


Semantic layer: Snowflake semantic views or Databricks metric views, imported through data_source()


The two warehouse objects above supply trusted metrics and dimensions: Snowflake calls them semantic views; Databricks calls them metric views. commons imports these through the data source, so they do not require a separate semantic_layer() call.
Warehouse models need not supply only calculations: the Databricks integration also imports descriptive context from metric views. Do not present warehouse metadata and context as mutually exclusive categories.

Context: warehouse models can also supply descriptive information. Add additional information to Markdown files and data dictionaries

Build
Trusted only mode

commons <- commons(
  data_sources = data_source(trials = trials),
  semantic_layer = semantic_layer("R/measures.R"),
  context_layer = context_layer(files = "context/protocol-conventions.md")
)

agent <- agent(
  ellmer::chat_anthropic(),
  commons = commons,
  mode = "trusted only"
)


Answers come only from trusted calculations
When no trusted calculation answers the question, the agent says so rather than writing its own SQL or R


mode = “trusted only” restricts the agent to trusted paths. It never receives run_sql or run_r, so it cannot write custom code, and because every answer comes from a trusted calculation, answers carry no provenance markers. The agent must have at least one trusted calculation.
Contrast with the default, “normal” mode: the agent prefers trusted calculations but falls back to writing its own SQL and R when none applies. Trusted only is useful when a strict, auditable boundary matters more than coverage, e.g. for regulated or externally shared numbers. It can also be a starting point: deploy in trusted only mode, review trajectories, and widen the trusted scope over time.

Deploy

Deploy like any other Shiny app.
(Optional) Enable built in trajectory-logging.
Enforce access with warehouse permissions and per-viewer credentials.


Create DBI connections and the agent inside the Shiny server for each session, using Connect viewer OAuth. The supplied connection enforces warehouse row-level security and table- and column-level policies.

Improve: analyze trajectories

commons(log = TRUE) records conversation histories with OpenTelemetry.
trajectory_read() reads trajectories from Connect or local traces.
trajectory_review() opens a Shiny app to browse, flag, and annotate conversations.


We’ll demo the trajectory reviewer here. Reviewed conversations surface recurring questions, then you add trusted calculations or context. The goal is to improve the system, not just ask users to check answers more carefully. These reviewer functions are in the R package.
Go to trajectory reviewer

Code as the foundation

LLMs are good at writing code
Reproducible, transparent, auditable


the primary thing, that might seem obvious but isn’t always obvious is that the model needs to write code
as much as possible, get it to write code does the agent have to run code? no – it could do things “in its head,” but then you lose reproducibility and transparency.
llms are good at code
we’ve learned from years of code for analysis that code is great for this
